author: Morgan Busby
title: Lawsuit against Bridgewater Foundation is going to mediation | The Vermont Standard
text:
A civil lawsuit filed by two prominent Central Vermont businessmen who say they were improperly removed from the board of directors for the Bridgewater Area Community Foundation Inc. will be headed to mediation in an effort to settle the dispute.
Charles Shackleton and Collen Doyle filed the civil action in Vermont Superior Court on Jan. 5 primarily against BACF Executive Director Kristiana Birmingham, of Woodstock, and board president Brian Bontrager, along with Treasurer John Hiers, both of Bridgewater Corners.
Also named as defendants in the lawsuit were four local people who reportedly were added to the foundation board recently: Blaise Biller and Jordan Camp, both of Woodstock, Malena Agin of Bridgewater, and Noelle Nunes of Bridgewater Corners, according to court filings.
The plaintiffs have agreed to drop Biller and Camp from the lawsuit after they submitted their resignations to the foundation board. Judge Kerry Ann McDonald-Cady has signed off on dropping both of them from the legal fight.
Woodstock lawyer Kaveh S. Shahi, who represents the two plaintiffs, had told the Vermont Standard when the case was filed that his clients were willing to drop the legal claims against any of the named defendants if they resigned from the board. Biller and Camp took the offer thus far.
Defendants in civil lawsuits in Vermont normally have 21 days to file a written response, but none had submitted their written answer disputing the claims by the end of January.
Instead, the two sides are headed to mediation with Middlebury lawyer Michael Marks presiding.
Mediation was first set for May 6, but a jury trial for Shahi bumped the date. Mediation is now set for June 10, court records show.
Judge McDonald-Cady did agree with a stipulation from both sides that the defendants would have until June 24 to file their written answers to the lawsuit.
The hope is with an early dispute resolution that judicial resources can be conserved, court papers note.
Former Deputy Attorney General Joshua Diamond was brought in during March to defend Birmingham, court papers show. The stipulated motion asks that Diamond be given time to get up to speed.
But he said this week, the defendants are ready for a fight.
“The Board vigorously disputes the allegations contained in the Complaint and will defend in the normal course of litigation,” Diamond told the Vermont Standard.
Attorneys Rachel L. Seelig, Megan E. Grove and Malachi T. Brennan of the SRH law firm in Burlington also were hired by the foundation’s insurance company to represent the other defendants.
BACF, which is a Vermont nonprofit formed in August 2018, is considered a “nominal defendant” in the case.
The lawsuit seeks both declaratory and injunctive relief that would declare that:
— The proper board of directors is Shackleton, Doyle, Bontrager, Hiers and Wendy Jenne, who were in place as of Jan. 1, 2025.
— The board has lawful authority over BACF’s operations, employees and assets and should be able to meet and act promptly to reestablish clear oversight and control over the organization.
— The original BACF bylaws adopted in 2018 remain in effect and must be followed until the proper Foundation board legally amends them.
— Any actions of the temporary Foundation board members since Jan. 13, 2025 be rejected and have no legal force or authority. That is the date that Birmingham reportedly said amended bylaws were adopted by the board that among other things allowed the president to unilaterally remove a director without a board vote or meeting.
Vermont law allows a director to be removed without cause, but only by a two-thirds vote of the directors in office, the lawsuit said.
According to the lawsuit, the BACF Board had voted unanimously to hire Wendy Banbury as its executive director in July 2025, and she was initially paid. However, Banbury began to question BACF finances, similar to those inquiries by some board members. Birmingham, who was still in control of financial accounts and payroll, stopped paying Banbury and said her hiring was invalid, the lawsuit said.
Birmingham, who plaintiffs claim had produced other fake documents, provided a copy of a purported contract naming her BACF’s executive director, effective Jan. 1, 2025, with a five-year term and a significant increase in salary and benefits, the lawsuit said.
Shackleton and Doyle maintain the contract was never presented at a board meeting for approval and contradicts an email by Birmingham in May 2025 that she says she was not the executive director.
The board would never have hired Banbury in July 2025 if Birmingham had been approved to serve for 5 years in that post just two months earlier, the lawsuit notes.
“Defendant Birmingham fabricated her employment agreement and gave herself a $40,000 raise without the knowledge of or approval by the plaintiffs,” the lawsuit said.
Shackleton said the plaintiffs should have taken action sooner. “We asked for transparency for many months. There was always some reason given that more time was needed,” Shackleton said.
For more on this, please see our May 21 edition of the Vermont Standard.
